newsitem.title: USA: Voters would forgo tax cuts - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Voters would forgo tax cuts - Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

A large majority of U.S. voters would be willing to forgo tax cuts in order to balance the federal budget while preserving key social programmes, according to a Reuters opinion poll issued on Thursday.
The poll of 1,008 registered voters, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International Jan. 25-29, carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

As President Bill Clinton prepares to deliver his State of the Union address next Tuesday, the poll found voters evenly split on his performance, with 49.6 percent rating it excellent or good and 49.8 percent saying it was fair or poor.
With Clinton due to send his budget to Congress next Thursday, the survey carried clues about the way voters feel about national priorities.
Voters clearly want to preserve social programmes, especially Medicare, which provides health insurance for senior citizens, and Medicaid, which provides help for the old, sick and poor.
By a margin of 69 to 19 percent, respondents said they would forgo tax cuts in order to preserve Medicare and other programmes while balancing the budget.

In general, a sense of optimism reigns. Nearly 54 percent of respondents felt the United States was heading in the right direction and only one in seven were pessimistic about their own personal finances.
However, the poll suggested that voters had little faith that government could deal with some of the most pressing issues facing the country.
"There seem to be a good deal of contradictions within the minds of voters," said pollster John Zogby.
"They are generally pleased with the country's direction and their own financial future, but see little hope of resolving a number of issues they care about deeply," he said.
Voters seemed slightly more confident about Clinton's ability to deal with problems than they were about the Republican-controlled Congress.
Respondents were asked to rank key issues in importance. Top of the list was reducing crime, which 86 percent felt was most or very important. Next, with 83 percent, was fixing Medicare and Medicaid.

Third on the list of priorities with 78 percent was cracking down on drugs; fourth with 76 percent was balancing the budget. Some 71 percent of respondents gave high priority to a health care reform plan, while 66 percent wanted to see a plan to clean up electoral campaign finances.
Sixty percent wanted action to protect the rights of minorities and women and 55 percent wanted the government to provide tax credits for college tuition, a favourite Clinton initiative.
Asked how they viewed the President, 65 percent of respondents said their overall impression of him was favourable, against 34 percent who viewed him unfavourably.
Vice President Al Gore, a probable candidate for the presidency in 2000, had a slightly better rating. Just over 67 percent viewed him favourably while 26 percent viewed him unfavourably.

Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who this month was reprimanded by the House and told to pay a $300,000 penalty for ethical violations, had a 63 percent unfavourable rating and a 28 percent favourable score.

On foreign affairs, respondents were asked whether the United States should respond to foreign crises by acting alone, or in concert with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), or with the United Nations.
Only seven percent favoured the U.S. going it alone while 42 percent favoured action with the United Nations and 35 percent supported action with NATO.
